source.title: Exploring Multilingual Probing in Large Language Models: A Cross-Language Analysis
source.authors: Daoyang Li; Haiyan Zhao; Qingcheng Zeng; Mengnan Du

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure text is garbled, but the paper's prose states the relevant similarity findings.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports cross-language similarity of probing vectors within LLMs, a related measure, but it does not test alignment between independently trained models or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study measures similarities between language-specific probing vectors, not similarity between model representations. Its probing-accuracy results are not rows for this claim. Figure-only values are not extracted where the text gives no specific outcome.
record.test_reason: The study trains linear probes per language inside each of five LLMs and compares the probe weight vectors across languages. It never compares the representations of different models, seeds or modalities. It does not test the claim; it neither tests nor relies on representational convergence. The record's relation 'tests' is inconsistent with its own T6 tranche; the correct relation is cites_only/none.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also say models may not learn deeper linguistic concepts effectively across all languages.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes multilingual probing vectors rather than reproducing a method for measuring alignment between independently trained models.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different similarity patterns across languages, layers, and datasets, but does not test alternative similarity metrics or settings as a sensitivity analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Within each LLM, linear probe vectors for high-resource languages correlate strongly with English and with each other, for example German and French above 0.6 in Qwen-1.8B. Low-resource languages (Tamil, Telugu, Oriya) stay below about 0.3. The paper says the pattern holds across Qwen and Gemma sizes and both datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a multilingual LLM, task-probe directions are shared across high-resource languages but not across low-resource languages.

record.problems: The study tests only five open-source models and two datasets. It translates English prompts and data into other languages with machine translation, which the authors note may introduce noise. It uses only linear probing. Similarity results are largely qualitative in the prose, and no uncertainty estimates or controls are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Probing accuracy findings were left out because they do not measure representational similarity. Figure-only similarity values without a textual description were not extracted.

untested.parts: No cross-model alignment, and no scale trend in alignment.
No vision models or paired image-caption data.
No mapping or stitching between models.
No metric or input sensitivity of model-to-model convergence.
No plateau test and no analysis of what causes model-to-model alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The relation should be cites_only rather than tests; the study does not engage the claim at all. The size-sweep across Qwen 0.5B/1.8B/7B concerns within-model cross-language probe similarity, not cross-model alignment, so it says nothing about V1.

versions.untested_parts: No scale sweep of alignment between independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representations.
No comparison across initialization seeds or shared-feature/subspace analysis.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test between models.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are identified across models.

The study uses probing-vector correlations and cosine similarity across languages and datasets, but does not test whether model-to-model convergence depends on similarity-measure settings or inputs, or vanishes out of distribution.
No test of whether model-to-model alignment plateaus or is explained by shared training data or objectives.
